A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SeedVR2. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original restoration benchmarks, training ablations, inference timings and a three-expert user study involving 50 videos.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds temporal evaluations, distillation comparisons, concurrent-method comparisons and sampling-step analyses.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 retain the adaptive window attention, progressive distillation, 3B/7B models and adversarial training losses. The additional optimizer, sampler and distillation-target specifications document the existing procedure without establishing a method change.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same training-data coverage and evaluate SPMCS, UDM10, REDS30, YouHQ40, VideoLQ and AIGC28. The added comparisons remain within this restoration coverage; heavy degradations and large motions illustrated in v2 were already reported as encountered conditions in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct one-step competitors: DOVE-5B in Table 7 and Figures 6/9, and DLoRAL in Figure 11. It also introduces a distillation-only comparator in Table 5/Figure 8 and bicubic comparisons in Table 4. The original benchmark comparator set remains intact.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 adds warping error and VMAF, and applies the existing no-reference metrics to synthetic benchmarks. Figure 10 introduces evaluations at 5, 10, 25 and 50 sampling steps, supplementing the retained fixed-50-step comparisons. The new distillation-only comparison explicitly matches training iterations.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled comparison of adversarial post-training against distillation alone, temporal-profile analysis, sampling-step sensitivity curves and challenging-condition case studies. These examine the benefit of adversarial training, temporal consistency and quality under reduced sampling budgets. The original attention and loss ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The added tables and curves continue the existing practice of reporting point estimates without uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the inference-time results are retained; 24.185 becoming 24.19 is rounding. New results include VideoLQ MUSIQ of 45.57 for distillation alone versus 51.09 for Ours-3B in Table 5. Table 7 shows Ours-3B outperforming DOVE-5B on NIQE/MUSIQ but trailing on CLIP-IQA/DOVER on both VideoLQ and AIGC28.

T1.justification: The adaptive-window and loss equations (1)–(4) are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or mathematical derivation is introduced; the added metric and distillation discussions are empirical or explanatory.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the claim of avoiding dependence on any teacher models or frozen priors and avoiding their bias to adversarial training without frozen priors that may alleviate bias. The abstract, principal contributions and conclusion retain the same one-step restoration, quality and speed claims.

C2.justification: Appendix A.2 extends the existing metric–perception discussion with an explanation of why reference misalignment can disadvantage generative restoration under warping error. It also elaborates the connection between distillation losses and oversmoothing. The VAE bottleneck, heavy-degradation failures and oversharpening limitations already appeared in v1.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the flow-matching target, noise schedule, Euler sampler/CFG and AdamW settings, including learning rate 1e-6 and weight decay 0.01. Section 7 adds PyTorch 2.4.0/CUDA 12.4 and promises code/checkpoints upon acceptance; v1 discussed releasing weights and validation sets. These disclosures do not establish changed training or an actual release.

R1.justification: Appendices A.4 and A.6 substantially extend positioning to direct concurrent one-step video-restoration methods. They distinguish SeedVR2 from DOVE's VAE adaptation and pixel-domain training, and DLoRAL's parameter-efficient tuning of a largely frozen prior. This materially supplements v1's emphasis on image-restoration acceleration and multi-step video methods.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main methodological narrative remain intact, with limited wording and author-note changes. Citations switch to author–year format, limitations and societal impacts move into main-text sections, and the appendices are reorganized around additional evaluations and comparisons.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual evidence through temporal profiles, challenging examples, distillation/concurrent-method comparisons, an eight-panel sampling-step figure and three new tables. Existing Figure 5 and Table 4 become Figure 7 and Table 6; the latter corrects the smaller model's header to Ours-3B. Retained displays and document typography are also reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central one-step restoration claims. Sampling-step curves address questions left open by v1's fixed-50-step comparisons, while matched-iteration distillation and concurrent one-step comparisons directly test the approach's value. Temporal evaluations and additional implementation details improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Table 4 introduces inconsistent warping-error labeling, but this limited presentation defect does not outweigh the substantive evidential gains.
